MINI_GAMES.name: How Deep? How High?
MINI_GAMES.desc: Guess the real depth or height — closest wins!

items.name: Depth to Earth's core
items.desc: How far below your feet does the liquid outer core begin?
items.note: The core–mantle boundary is about 2,900 km down. The mantle is the thickest layer of Earth.

items.name: Distance to the center of Earth
items.desc: From the surface straight down to the very middle of the inner core
items.note: Earth's average radius is about 6,371 km. The deepest hole people ever drilled reached only about 12 km.

items.name: Depth of the Mariana Trench
items.desc: Challenger Deep, the deepest point in the ocean
items.note: Challenger Deep is about 10,900 to 11,000 m deep (measurements vary a little). Drop Mount Everest in and its peak would still be about 2 km underwater.

items.name: Height of Borah Peak
items.desc: Idaho's tallest mountain, in the Lost River Range
items.note: Borah Peak is 12,662 ft tall. The 1983 magnitude 6.9 earthquake raised it about a foot.

items.name: Height of Mount Everest
items.desc: Earth's highest point above sea level
items.note: A 2020 survey by China and Nepal measured Everest at 8,849 m, and it's still rising a few millimeters a year.

MINI_GAMES.name: Mohs Hardness Test
MINI_GAMES.desc: Guess each mineral's hardness on the Mohs scale (1–10)!

items.name: Quartz
items.desc: The most common mineral in sand. It scratches glass easily.
items.note: Quartz is a 7. That's why sandy grit scratches glass (about 5.5) and steel.

items.name: Calcite
items.desc: The mineral that makes up limestone and marble. It fizzes in acid.
items.note: Calcite is a 3. A copper penny (about 3) is about as hard, and a steel nail scratches it.

items.name: Talc
items.desc: Soft, soapy-feeling mineral used in baby powder
items.note: Talc is a 1, the softest mineral on the scale. Your fingernail (about 2.5) scratches it.

items.name: Topaz
items.desc: A gemstone mineral, Utah's state gem
items.note: Topaz is an 8. Only corundum (9) and diamond (10) are harder on the scale.

items.name: Fluorite
items.desc: Colorful cubic crystals; many glow under UV light
items.note: Fluorite is a 4. The word 'fluorescent' comes from this mineral.

MINI_GAMES.name: Idaho by the Numbers
MINI_GAMES.desc: Real Idaho Earth science numbers — how close can you get?

items.name: Bruneau Dunes
items.desc: Height of the tallest single-structured sand dune in North America
items.note: The big dune at Bruneau Dunes State Park is about 470 ft tall.

items.name: Shoshone Falls
items.desc: How far the Snake River drops at the 'Niagara of the West' near Twin Falls
items.note: Shoshone Falls drops about 212 ft. That's taller than Niagara Falls (about 167 ft).

items.name: Snake River Plain Aquifer
items.desc: How much of southern Idaho this groundwater reservoir stretches under
items.note: The aquifer stretches under about 10,800 square miles and supplies drinking water and irrigation for much of southern Idaho.

items.name: Old Faithful
items.desc: Average time between eruptions of Yellowstone's famous geyser, just next door
items.note: Old Faithful erupts about every 90 minutes on average. Groundwater heated by the Yellowstone hotspot builds pressure until it blasts out.

items.name: Craters of the Moon
items.desc: How long ago its most recent lava eruptions happened
items.note: Craters of the Moon last erupted only about 2,000 years ago — and the area could erupt again.

MINI_GAMES.name: Bigger or Smaller?
MINI_GAMES.desc: Compare two Earth science giants — pick the right answer!

items.q: Measured from its base to its peak, which mountain is taller?
opts: Mauna Kea (from its base on the sea floor)
items.fact: Mauna Kea rises over 10,000 m from its base on the sea floor, taller than Everest. Everest still wins for height above sea level.

items.q: Which seismic wave travels faster through Earth?
opts: They all travel at the same speed
items.fact: P waves are fastest, so they always reach a seismograph first. S waves are next, then surface waves.

items.q: Carbon dioxide in the air was about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution and about 427 ppm in 2025. That's about...
items.fact: 427 ÷ 280 ≈ 1.5. That's about a 50% increase, mostly from burning fossil fuels.

items.q: About how many Earths could fit inside the Sun?
items.fact: The Sun's volume could hold about 1.3 million Earths. Its diameter is about 109 times Earth's.
